explanations.answer: They multiply until the land is filled with them
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Verse 7 says the Israelites were fruitful, increased rapidly and became exceedingly numerous, “…so that the land was filled with them.” Verse 5 counts seventy descendants of Jacob, and now the land is packed. That's a family reunion that got WAY out of hand.

explanations.answer: They dwindle down to just a few families
explanations.explanation: I get the guess. When a whole generation passes away, you'd think things would get quiet. But verse 7 says the opposite: they multiplied and became exceedingly numerous. The text says “…so that the land was filled with them.”

explanations.answer: They pack up and head back to Canaan
explanations.explanation: Jacob's family did come into Egypt from Canaan (Genesis 46:6). But nothing in this passage has them heading back. Verse 7 says the land was filled with them, so they stay and keep growing. I don't see a moving truck anywhere in this chapter.

That's right, baker. In verse 9 the king tells his people, “the Israelites have become too numerous and too powerful for us.” Then he says, “Come, let us deal shrewdly with them, or they will increase even more…” I think a growing crowd has him rattled. That's the whole plan, and it's not a kind one.

Close, but the text says otherwise. The king tells his people that the Israelites have become too numerous and too powerful for them (Exodus 1:9). His plan is right there in verse 10: “Come, let us deal shrewdly with them, or they will increase even more…” So the statement is true as written.

explanations.answer: Fight for Egypt's enemies and leave the country
explanations.explanation: You've got it. The king says if a war breaks out, “…they may join our enemies, fight against us, and leave the country.” That's three worries stacked in one sentence. He's picturing the worst case before anything has even happened.

explanations.answer: Hide out in the hills until the war ends
explanations.explanation: That one sounds sensible, but it's not what the king says. His fear is bigger than hiding. He says they may “…join our enemies, fight against us, and leave the country.” Nothing about hills or waiting it out.

explanations.answer: Refuse to send Egypt a single soldier
explanations.explanation: Staying out of it would be one thing. But the king's fear is that they'd go further than that. In verse 10 he says they may “…join our enemies, fight against us, and leave the country.” That's joining the other side, not sitting this one out.

That's the word, friend. Verse 11 says the Egyptians appointed taskmasters over the Israelites to oppress them with forced labor. These are the ones standing over the work and pushing. It's a hard picture, and the text doesn't soften it.

Shepherds look after sheep, and that's not what's happening in verse 11. The Egyptians appoint taskmasters over the Israelites to oppress them with forced labor. Nobody is leading anybody to green pastures here.

Scribes are the writing folks, and verse 11 doesn't mention any. What it says is that the Egyptians appointed taskmasters over the Israelites to oppress them with forced labor. It's about overseers of work, not paperwork.
Yes, baker. Verse 11 says the forced labor built Pithom and Rameses as store cities for Pharaoh. Pharaoh is the title for Egypt's king. These two cities were built by the Israelites' own hands.
Nice try, but those two belong to a later book. Jericho and Ai turn up in Joshua (Joshua 6:1; 8:1). The store cities in Exodus 1:11 are Pithom and Rameses.

Those two names do show up together, friend. Genesis 10:11 lists Nineveh and Calah in the same list, with Rehoboth-Ir between them. But the store cities the Israelites built for Pharaoh in Exodus 1:11 are Pithom and Rameses.

That's what you'd expect, baker. If you squeeze a group harder, you'd think it shrinks. But verse 12 says, “But the more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied and flourished…” So the statement has it backwards.

Right, it's False. Verse 12 says, “But the more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied and flourished…” The pressure goes up and the numbers go up with it. The king's plan is doing the opposite of what he wanted.

That's the one. Verse 12 says the Egyptians came to dread the Israelites. The Israelites keep multiplying and flourishing, and the Egyptians dread them. I think the king's plan landed him somewhere he didn't plan to be.

That would be a softer ending, friend, but it's not what the text says. In verse 12 the Egyptians came to dread the Israelites. And verses 13-14 say they worked the Israelites ruthlessly, and every service they imposed was harsh.
Trust would change the whole story, but verse 12 doesn't go there. It says the Egyptians came to dread the Israelites. And in verse 13 they keep working them ruthlessly.

Yes. Verse 14 says they “…made their lives bitter with hard labor in brick and mortar, and with all kinds of work in the fields.” Then it adds, “Every service they imposed was harsh.” This is a heavy part of the story, and the text says it plainly.
I see why you'd pick it, since the work was hard. But verse 14 doesn't say their lives were made short. It says they “…made their lives bitter with hard labor in brick and mortar…”

That's a hard feeling, but it's not the word in the text. Verse 14 says they “…made their lives bitter with hard labor in brick and mortar, and with all kinds of work in the fields.” The word is bitter.

I can see why you'd think it, since the king is the one giving orders. But verse 17 says the midwives “…did not do as the king of Egypt had instructed; they let the boys live.” Shiphrah and Puah were told one thing and did another.

Right, baker. Verse 17 says the midwives “…did not do as the king of Egypt had instructed; they let the boys live.” Shiphrah and Puah were told one thing and did another. That takes some serious courage.

That's it, friend. Verse 17 says the midwives feared God and did not do as the king had instructed. The king of Egypt gave an order, and these two women heard it and just didn't do it. The text says why: they feared God. I think that took real courage.
The text doesn't give a reward as the reason. Verse 17 says it was because they feared God. God does bless them later (Exodus 1:20-21), but that comes after, not as why they did it.
The text doesn't point that way. Verse 17 says they “…did not do as the king of Egypt had instructed…” The reason it gives is that they feared God.

Yes, baker. The king summons the midwives and asks, “Why have you done this? Why have you let the boys live?” Then in verse 19 the midwives answer Pharaoh, “The Hebrew women are not like the Egyptian women, for they are vigorous and give birth before a midwife arrives.” Both parts match the text.

Both parts of this one match the text. In verse 18 the king asks, “Why have you done this? Why have you let the boys live?” In verse 19 the midwives answer that the Hebrew women are vigorous and give birth before a midwife arrives. So it's True.

Right. Verse 20 says God was good to the midwives, and the people multiplied and became even more numerous. Shiphrah and Puah feared God, and God was good to them. It's worth noticing who the verse names.

That's not who the verse names, friend. Verse 20 says God was good to the midwives, and the people multiplied and became even more numerous. The Egyptians are the ones giving the harsh orders in this passage.
Levi is one of the sons on the list in verse 2, but Levites aren't named in this verse. Verse 20 says God was good to the midwives. Those are Shiphrah and Puah, the ones who feared God.

You've got it, baker! Verse 21 says, “And because the midwives feared God, He gave them families of their own.” Shiphrah and Puah spent their work helping Hebrew women give birth, and then God gave them families of their own. I think that's about the sweetest ending a midwife could get. I'd be hugging every one of them with my mustache.
Goshen is a real place in this story. Pharaoh once told Joseph to settle his family there (Genesis 47:6). But verse 21 doesn't say land. It says God “…gave them families of their own.”
Flocks would be a nice gift, but verse 21 doesn't mention them. It says, “And because the midwives feared God, He gave them families of their own.” That's the gift the text names.
